item.title: Gas leak and leek gas
item.description:
An army of maintenance staff, various contraptions slung across their shoulders, barged into my tiny NYC apartment alarmed by my complaint: the stove was leaking gas. Their contraptions however reported nothing. All good, bye-bye. The sun set and the sun rose and once again the ominous vapors of gas came knocking at my nostrils; once again, the army came knocking at my door, and once again, nothing.

But I was no mad man imagining things. I traced with my own superhuman snout every surface and every ridge of my kitchen, turning it inside out, turning my own lungs inside out, certain that the cuplrit would eventually graze the tip of my nose, which it did.

My apartment, I discovered, was not on the brink of an explosion. It was being lovingly fondled by the sloppy breath of garlic, periodically exhaled by a (washed) jar of garlic paste (that I had just added to my precious recycled jar collection).

But why would garlic reek of natural gas? I ran to The Computer: O, dear! What gives natural gas its odor?. The Computer said “Aye, Aye Captain, what you seek are organosulphuric additives called mercaptans!”. When did they begin doing this? In 1937, a school in Texas went up in flames taking with it the lives of hundreds of students and teachers. In a shocking turn of events, lawmakers did something to protect school students within a span of a few weeks, which was to enforce odorization of natural gas. President Roosevelt received a sympathetic telegram from er… the then leader of Germany. See photo.

Then, pray tell, from what does garlic take its smell? The Computer said “Mr. Alice-in-Wonderland, your rabbit hole has led you to the organosulfuric allicin, emitted in defense by garlic crushed.”

The link between the two I would find at the end of another rabbit hole: the oesophagus. Allicin, trapped in the stomach, breaks down into vapours of allyl mercaptan (aha!) that is released out into broad daylight as garlic breath.

Just as the case was being closed, another bulb lit up: does allyl have anything to do with the genus that garlic and its odorous, bulbous siblings (onions, leeks, shallots and chives) belong to: allium? The Computer nodded. An allyl derivative, it seems, was first extracted from garlic oil, thus obtaining that name, much like how the “but-" in “butane” comes from (rancid) butter (latin: butyrum) from which butyric acid was first derived.

Allyl’s well that end’s well?

item.title: Cunk on Budapest
item.description:
Budapest is a city so wondrous that it makes you wonder: what is Budap? Is there a city more Budap than this, or as the name advertises, is this really the Budapest of all cities?

The first thing to watch in Budapest is a river called The Danube, which is modeled after a river that flows through Vienna: The Danube. This has greatly confounded river scientists and philosophers alike, because no one knows which is the The Danube.

What we do understand is that this The Danube has actually sliced the city into two halves. The half I stand on is called Pest, and the half that I’m looking at is called Buda.

Before they discovered the real name of the combined city, the ancients, who couldn’t be arsed to look at a real atlas, referred to the city as Pest-Buda. That is because they were looking at where I’m standing, standing where I’m looking at.

Modern historians now know that was the wrong way to look and stand, which is how the phrase “to stand corrected” was coined. Modern historians also discovered after carefully listening to recordings of Hungarians that Pest is pronounced “Pesht”, a discovery made possible by the invention of voice recorders.

Looking across at “Pesht”, standing in Buda, is the gigantic statue of St Gellert, a 11th century Christian man hired by the king to evangelize the pagan peasants . But because it would be many centuries before the Christians would invent the television, the pagans of those ancient times could reciprocate in person by rolling Mr. Gellert down the hill in a barrel filled with nails.

This brings us to another pronunciation tidbit which is that at that moment, St Gellert was pronounced dead.

We are now in front of the magnificient Hotel Corinthia Budapest that inspired the iconic mother-child director duo, Wes and her son to direct the movie The “The Grand Budapest Hotel”, a remake of the first ever hotel movie with freaks in it, The “The Shining”, but disappointingly, the remake was abridged for the cowards.

The grandest architecture in the city is right here in this very living room situated somewhere in The Hungarian parliament. The little guide man in my handheld Nokia audio-brick tells me this room is lined by a “whopping 40 kilogram of gold”, which is interesting until you realize that 40 kilograms is barely anything, and no scientist knows what a “whopping” is to this date.

The little man also says that this XXL building is built symmetrically reflecting what was a “bicameral” government until War 2, which is encouraging news, since that means I can just imagine the other half of it and give my legs a [censored] break.

Two mysteries remain as I exit these grand political living quarters. Since War 2, Hungary has been a “unicameral” government: how do they guard all this gold with one camera? To add to the mystery, as of 2024, which is the times as I speak, no one is sure who the lead man of this building is. Is it Viktor or Ban?

Once you step out of the building, you will notice two things: broad daylight and then immediate darkness as you faint from the sudden daylight. You will then wake up right next to an installation of the great mummy of the great US president who was involved in the falldown of communism in Hungary. It is the great insert-adjective Ronald Reagus, named after the economic policies of his time, Reaganomics, an economics which has been penetrating our societies for years and will do so for years to come.

Note: An instance of the word “[censored]” had to be censored from the last line to be in line with latest legal laws of these times.

All photos are mine except for the one of that hotel.

item.title: Cunk on Salzburg
item.description:
Geolocated in the country of Austria is the city of Salzburg—the name, a portmanteau of the German food item “salt" and an American delicacy of Germanic origins called “hamburger”, which the city of Hamburg was strangely named after even though the Germans themselves ingest hamburgers only in an efficient smoothie formula called “beer”.

Very close to Salzburg is the picturesqueue village of Hallstatt, where you can watch hundreds of tourists queue up for pictures. Interestingly, the name Hallstatt is likely anonymous with Salzburg—it also means “salt settlement”—but as linguists point out, it is spelled differently from Salzburg.

This village long used to be a postcard village. But then postcards were eradicated after people discovered that a postcard is just a boring sheet of paper that also exposes your intimate messages and address to anyone. Which is why this has now become an “Instagram village”: an Instagram is much more fascinating to the brain and does not reveal your messages and addresses to anyone but a select few, like the people who want to sell you things and the Government.

Salzburg is the location that spawned a music artist revered by anyone who pretends to understand Western classical music: the composer Wolfgang Amadeus Mode’s Art, a man who released many back-to-back tracks to become the top 10 most played artists on the music charts of those days, which was probably an engraved wall in the middle of the town.

It is a shame that before Mode could try his luck on the world wide internet, Mode gave up on composing music altogether at the age of 35, soon after he released his last breath in 1791. Like the other dead composers of his time, he then began dabbling in what is called as decomposing.

Fast forward to this day, Austrians take such immense pride in Mode’s Art’s Art that they honor him by peddling these palm-sized balls of chocolate with his face on it. These sobering edibles are called Mozartkugel, which in native Austrian means “Mode’s Art’s Balls”.

Now, as you walk along Salzburg, you’ll notice a river flowing through, its name pronounced exactly like the French novelist Balzac, but with an “s”: Salzach. Since its name rings a familiar bell, they did not bother to prefix a “the” behind it like they do to the The Danube. But they do suffix the word “river” after it, just in case you forget what we’re talking about.

One of the other distinctive hanging features of Salzburg are these metal designs hung in front of every shop, visually telling you what their business model is, like the logo of the American hire-a-mermaid shop, Starbucks, or the like the logo of the googling machine, Google.

These “guilds” date back to the mediaeval times when most peasants in the feudal system were too illiterate to even spell the times they chose to be in. Literacy was then a luxury of the powerful, unlike our egalitarian modern times, where anyone can become a well-read billionaire for free.

Speaking of billionaires, in upcoming documentary, we will travel from the city of Salzburg to the modern city of Zuckerberg: San Frances and Co.

item.title: Planets, Dharma and Disaster
item.description:
Every celestial object sails across the sky during the course of a day. But our perceptive ancestors noticed that most do not move relative to each other. It was as if enclosing us earthlings was a mighty, solid, revolving dome—the firmament—and embedded on that ever-turning dome were tiny ever-glowing crystals—the stars—frozen in place.The firmament, a biblical term, finds linguistic kinship in the East: in the Sanskrit word dharma (a complex term that, among many things, means cosmic order, law, duty), and also in the word dharti (the earth). The firmament, dharma and dharti, as their ancient root *dher- suggests, are all a form of support or maintenance, one imaginary, one abstract, and one real.The “fa-dha” kinship parallels the one between the words related to smoke, the Latin fuma and the Sanskrit dhūma.

Our ancestors, staring in wonder at these crystals of light, dreamt of lines connecting them to form shapes, the constellations. These constellations, memorable and recognizable like paintings decorating the inner walls of the dome, reliably guided our ancestors in navigating and ploughing the earth. Reliable they were, because as the dome rotated, so did the stars, but always only as a whole, keeping solid and intact the paintings in our ancestors’ imagination. Some shapes disappeared every dawn overwhelmed by the deluge of sunlight, but they still revealed themselves the next night, solid and intact;These are the circumpolar constellations, like the big dipper, that orient one towards the north or the south. yet others might, one fine night, abandon the sky for months at length, but they still returned a few months later, solid and intact. These are the seasonal constellations, like the constellations along the zodiac belt, whose arrival in a year would mark the beginning or the end of a season.

But our perceptive ancestors noticed on this solid dome a handful of objects that moved relative even to the dome and its orderly stars. These objects, it seemed, possessed a will of their own: they were insubordinate to the rigid shapes, the cosmic order imposed by the human mind onto the heavens. These rebellious travelers of the celestial dome were named after the Greek planan (to wander, to lead astray, to deceive), to become known as the planets,It is imprecise to attribute the “wandering” in this etymology to simply the fact that a planet orbits the sun. It is their relative motion against the celestial map on the dome that gave rise to the idea of “wandering”. their refusal to fit into a constellation most prominent when observing them as they come closest to each other in the sky during what is called a conjunction.This picture of the celestial dome reframes our interpretation of the word disaster (dis + aster). Naively, it conjures the image of an ill-positioned and misaligned star. But in the celestial dome, the stars, which are forced into place on the distant walls of the dome, must themselves bear no fault for their positions; it is the planets, the apparently free-willed entities in the foreground, that must have wandered into an unwelcome constellation to spell disaster.
